ideas.title: Four years after Dobbs, more women in ban states don't know where to get an abortion: 53%, up from 43% in 2024
ideas.angle: Abortion by mail and shield-law telehealth have grown, but KFF finds women in ban states know less about where to go than they did two years ago. The story is the gap between what is available and what women know is available, and who falls into it: younger, lower-income and rural women, and those who don't know medication abortion exists.
ideas.why_now: New 2026 KFF Women's Health Survey, released Oct 26. It is the first national read on whether awareness is improving or eroding as ban-state access shifts to telehealth.
ideas.is_it_real: These are KFF's own survey numbers from an independent analysis, not an interested party's claim. The 53% vs 43% change is KFF's figure. A reporter should check sample size and margin for the ban-state subgroup before leaning on the 10-point change. The companion brief adds national estimates on experiences with abortion and knowledge of medication abortion.
ideas.primary_test: KFF 2026 Women's Health Survey topline and methodology (ban-state subgroup n and margin of error), paired with Society of Family Planning #WeCount data on telehealth abortion provision into ban states

items.title: Survey: More Than Half of Women in States with Abortion Bans Wouldn’t Know Where to Get an Abortion if They Needed One, Up Since 2024
items.summary: More than half (53%) of reproductive-age women living in states with abortion-provision bans say they would not know where to go or where to find information if they needed an abortion, up from 43% in 2024, according to a new KFF survey.

items.title: Women’s Experiences with Abortion, Access, and Concerns About Future Pregnancy
items.summary: This brief provides national estimates from the 2026 KFF Women’s Health Survey on reproductive age women’s experiences with abortion, the impact of Dobbs on abortion access and women’s concerns about future pregnancies, as well as women’s knowledge on the availability of medication abortion.

ideas.title: Is it real? Lymphatic drainage massage: what it does for lymphedema and post-surgery swelling vs. the TikTok 'depuff and detox' claims
ideas.angle: Manual lymphatic drainage has real clinical uses: lymphedema care, and the swelling after liposuction and body contouring, which she has been through herself after her body lift. Social media sells it for debloating, detox, cellulite and weight loss. The post checks each claim against the trial evidence and says where the receipts stop.
ideas.why_now: The massage therapists' trade association is pushing it during National Massage Therapy Awareness Week, and lymphatic drainage keeps trending as a wellness service. It's not urgent, so it can wait for a slower Wednesday after this week's two tfm picks.
ideas.is_it_real: The source is the American Massage Therapy Association, which has a stake in more massage bookings. The release itself says it separates benefit from hype, but the post has to rest on independent reviews, not AMTA's summary. The evidence on lymphedema is mixed even there, and evidence for the consumer claims is thin to absent.
ideas.primary_test: Cochrane and other systematic reviews of manual lymphatic drainage for lymphedema (including after breast cancer) and for post-operative swelling, compared against what wellness marketing claims

items.title: Manual Lymphatic Massage Is Growing in Popularity — Discover Its Benefits and What You Should Know
items.date_basis: within 1 day(s) of the digest run
items.summary: The American Massage Therapy Association reviews emerging evidence on lymphatic drainage, separating genuine clinical benefit from social-media hype during National Massage Therapy Awareness Week.

ideas.title: 4.3 million Medicare enrollees will lose their Advantage or Part D plan at year's end, and 1.4 million more are in plans being merged: check your mail before Dec 7
ideas.angle: A short, useful item for open enrollment: KFF's count from CMS data is 3.1 million Medicare Advantage drug plan enrollees and 1.2 million stand-alone Part D enrollees whose plans end, plus 1.4 million in consolidating plans. It tells readers what a non-renewal notice means and what their options are.
ideas.why_now: Open enrollment runs through Dec 7, and terminated plans end Dec 31. Pitching is blocked because this is already widely covered, but the number is usable this week.
ideas.is_it_real: These are KFF's analysis of CMS plan data, an independent source. Before running it, confirm the special enrollment period and Medigap guaranteed-issue rights for people whose plans are not renewed against CMS and Medicare.gov guidance. Don't state them from memory.

items.title: More Than 4 Million Medicare Beneficiaries Will Have Their Medicare Advantage or Stand-Alone Prescription Drug Plan Terminated at the End of 2026
items.summary: Data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) shows that 4.3 million Medicare beneficiaries, including 3.1 million Medicare Advantage drug plan enrollees and 1.2 million PDP enrollees, will have their plan terminated at the end of 2026. An additional 1.4 million Medicare Advantage enrollees are in a plan that is consolidating with another plan offered by the same insurer.
